rationale: No displayed earlier directive plausibly supplied a concrete, material drafting template. C24 and C04 both address the legal consequences of Alaska and Hawaii becoming States, but their operative machinery—updating territorial references and delegating statutory authority—is materially different from the child's rule treating assignments in those States as assignments outside the United States. C10 contains superficially similar deeming language and Defense-related regulatory administration, but applies a general definitional structure to military subsistence and lacks the child's statehood adjustment or periodic-review clause. These similarities are thematic or routine rather than evidence of reusable drafting.

shared_material.child_excerpt: Assignment of an employee to duty In the State of Alaska or Hawaii ... shall be held and considered ... to be an assignment to duty outside the United States.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: all of the provisions ... which refer to or applied to or within the Territory of Alaska or the Territory of Hawaii shall ... refer to or apply to or within the State of Alaska and the State of Hawaii, respectively.
shared_material.explanation: C24 shares the Alaska-and-Hawaii statehood context and uses a legal deeming adjustment, but it changes territorial references rather than classifying employee assignments and does not supply the child's administrative mechanism.

shared_material.child_excerpt: Assignment of an employee to duty In the State of Alaska or Hawaii under regulations prescribed pursuant to section 1586 of title 10
shared_material.parent_excerpt: The authority vested in the President by section 45(a) of the Alaska Omnibus Act ... [and] section 5(e) of the act ... providing for the admission of the State of Hawaii
shared_material.explanation: C04 concerns statutory consequences of Alaska and Hawaii statehood, but delegates unrelated property and reporting functions; the overlap does not extend to a parallel operative provision.
